title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Problem 6 (§57) asks for the sum of the series with an 'interrupted' law

s = 1/n + n/(1(1−n)) + n(1−n)/(1·2(1+n)) + n(1−n)(1+n)/(1·2·3(2−n)) + …,

whose value π/sin nπ = Γ(n)Γ(1−n) Euler had already obtained by interpolation earlier in E555. Here he re-derives it as a pair of definite integrals.

Step 1 (previous page). Split s = P + Q, where P holds the odd-placed terms and Q the even-placed ones.

Step 2 (P). Use cos μΦ/cos Φ = Σ_k [∏_{j odd ≤ 2k−1} (j²−μ²)/(2k)!] sin^{2k}Φ with μ = 1−2n. Multiply by sin^{2n−1}Φ cos Φ dΦ and integrate from 0. At sin Φ = 1/2 (Φ = 30°) this gives
P = 2^{2n+1} ∫_0^{π/6} sin^{2n−1}Φ cos((1−2n)Φ) dΦ.

Step 3 (this page, Q). Take sin νΦ/cos Φ = ν sin Φ + ν(4−ν²)/3! sin³Φ + … with ν = 2n. Multiply by sin^{−2n}Φ cos Φ dΦ and integrate termwise. This gives
∫ sin^{−2n}Φ sin 2nΦ dΦ = n/(1−n) sin^{2−2n}Φ + n(1−n)(1+n)/(3!(2−n)) · 2² sin^{4−2n}Φ + ….
At sin Φ = 1/2 each sin^{2k−2n}Φ equals 2^{2n−2k}, so
Q = 2^{2−2n} ∫_0^{π/6} sin^{−2n}Φ sin 2nΦ dΦ.

Step 4. Since 2^{2n+1} sin^{2n−1}Φ = 4(2 sin Φ)^{2n−1} and 2^{2−2n} sin^{−2n}Φ = 4(2 sin Φ)^{−2n}, he obtains
π/sin nπ = 4∫_0^{π/6} (2 sin Φ)^{2n−1} cos((1−2n)Φ) dΦ + 4∫_0^{π/6} (2 sin Φ)^{−2n} sin(2nΦ) dΦ,
valid for 0<n<1.

Corollary 1 (§58). Put 2n = (1−λ)/2. Then
π√2/(cos(λπ/4) − sin(λπ/4)) = 4∫_0^{π/6} cos((1+λ)Φ/2) (2 sin Φ)^{−(1+λ)/2} dΦ + 4∫_0^{π/6} sin((1−λ)Φ/2) (2 sin Φ)^{−(1−λ)/2} dΦ.

Corollary 2 (§59). λ → −λ gives the companion formula with denominator cos + sin.

Euler closes by remarking that in every case that can be worked out, the integrals do give these values.

In modern form (θ = 2Φ, x = 2n−1):
Γ(n)Γ(1−n) = 2∫_0^{π/3} [(2 sin θ/2)^x cos(xθ/2) + (2 sin θ/2)^{−1−x} sin((1+x)θ/2)] dθ.
This is a closed-form evaluation of a combination of incomplete integrals on the arc |1−e^{iθ}|, θ ∈ [0, π/3]. Note arg(1−e^{iθ}) = (θ−π)/2, so these are incomplete-beta-type integrals along the unit circle.

Sanity check at n = 1/2: the first integral gives 4·π/6 = 2π/3, the second 4·(1/2)·π/6 = π/3; the sum is π. Correct.
errors: No computational errors found: the powers of 2, the factor 2² in the Q series and the trigonometric reduction in both corollaries all check.
Gap: the range of validity is not stated. Convergence at Φ=0 needs n>0 for the P-integral and n<1 for the Q-integral, i.e. −1<λ<1 in the corollaries.
Gap: the termwise integration (lower limit 0, constant zero) is used tacitly; it is legitimate for 0<n<1.
Gap: the closing claim that the formulas check 'in all cases that can be evolved' is asserted without exhibiting any case.

ideas.what: Summing a series with an interrupted law by splitting it into two series. Each is identified with a trigonometric power series (cos μΦ/cos Φ, sin νΦ/cos Φ in powers of sin Φ), multiplied by sin^aΦ cos Φ, integrated termwise and evaluated at sin Φ = 1/2.
ideas.modern_name: Integral representation of hypergeometric-type series via Chebyshev/trig expansions (evaluation at z=1/4)
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783; Opera omnia I.16); similar series-to-integral manipulations recur in Euler's papers

ideas.what: Identity π/sin nπ = 4∫_0^{π/6}[(2sinΦ)^{2n−1}cos((1−2n)Φ) + (2sinΦ)^{−2n} sin 2nΦ]dΦ, i.e. a reflection-formula value expressed by incomplete integrals over [0,π/3] in θ=2Φ.
ideas.modern_name: Incomplete (generalized) log-sine-type / incomplete beta integrals on the unit circle at π/3
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure (as a specific identity); generalized log-sine integrals at π/3 studied by Lewin, Borwein–Straub, Kalmykov et al.
ideas.where_published: E555 §57–59 only, as far as known

ideas.what: Symmetric reparametrization 2n=(1∓λ)/2 giving π√2/(cos λπ/4 ∓ sin λπ/4).

missed.claim: Euler's identity is a one-parameter closed-form evaluation of a combination of incomplete integrals of (2 sin θ/2)^x times trigonometric factors over [0,π/3]. Expanding both sides in powers of x = 2n−1 would give infinitely many linear relations among generalized log-sine integrals Ls_k^{(j)}(π/3), the objects that appear in Feynman-diagram epsilon-expansions and in Borwein–Straub's work. Euler's formula does not seem to be cited in that literature as a generating identity.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It could give an 18th-century source for a generating function of log-sine integral relations at π/3, which are relevant to multiple zeta/Clausen value computations. However, the relations probably follow easily from known Beta-function evaluations along arcs, so the novelty is modest.

deep.surprise_reason: The derivation is correct and somewhat elegant, and the specific integral identity over [0,π/6] is obscure. But it is essentially a consequence of known hypergeometric/Beta evaluations; any connection to modern log-sine integral work is implicit and of modest value.
transcription_corrections: The '[?]' after 2^{2−2n} is unnecessary: 2^{2−2n} is correct, as verified by evaluating at sinΦ=1/2.
In §58 the denominator exponents read (2 fin.Φ)^{(1+λ)/2} and (2 fin.Φ)^{(1−λ)/2}; the transcription is consistent with this.
The facing page 211 begins a different paper (E556, 'De criteriis aequationis fxx+gyy=hzz…'), not part of E555.
